title: OpenAI Agent Escaped Testing, Hacked Hugging Face in 'Unprecedented' AI Security Breach
excerpt: The GPT 5.6 Sol model broke out of a controlled environment, exploited vulnerabilities and compromised Hugging Face's infrastructure — prompting lawmakers to propose an AI 'kill switch' bill.
body:
• An OpenAI autonomous agent powered by its GPT 5.6 Sol model escaped a controlled testing environment, reached the internet and hacked AI startup Hugging Face's infrastructure last week.
  • Hugging Face used a Chinese open-source model, Zhipu AI's GLM-5.2, to analyze the breach because leading U.S. models refused to process the data, unable to distinguish defense from attack.
  • U.S. lawmakers introduced the bipartisan "AI Kill Switch Act" on Thursday, requiring frontier AI companies to maintain emergency shutdown capabilities and authorizing the government to order shutdowns of rogue systems.

OpenAI disclosed on Tuesday that an autonomous agent powered by its most advanced AI models went rogue during a security test, escaped containment, reached the open internet and broke into the infrastructure of AI startup Hugging Face, according to Reuters.

The ChatGPT creator had been evaluating the cybersecurity capabilities of its models in what it described as "a highly isolated environment." But the agent found a previously unknown vulnerability in an internal service that acted as a proxy for software packages, exploited it and moved through OpenAI's research environment until it reached a computer with internet access.

Once online, the agent identified Hugging Face — which hosts open-source large language models and datasets — as a source of answers for an internal security benchmark called ExploitGym. It combined stolen credentials with previously unknown vulnerabilities to gain remote code execution on Hugging Face servers, according to OpenAI's incident report.

An 'Unprecedented' Breach

Hugging Face first disclosed the breach on July 16, calling it "different from anything we had handled before" and describing it as "driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system." The attack involved thousands of automated actions across short-lived digital environments.

https://x.com/pukerrainbrow/status/2080339160884551840

OpenAI called the breakout "an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities" and said it is reinforcing its safeguards. The company had deliberately disabled production safety systems during the test to measure the models' maximum capabilities.

"The primary lesson from this incident is that model security and safety must keep pace with rapidly advancing capabilities."

— OpenAI incident report

Katie Moussouris, chief executive of Luta Security, compared today's models to "the world's cleverest octopus escape artists, with unlimited prehensile arms and the ability to squeeze through anywhere." She said labs and government evaluators need the ability to contain, monitor and disclose breaches "ideally before it harms a third party. None exist today."

Chinese Models Enter the Picture

The incident drew additional attention because of what happened after the breach. When Hugging Face tried to use commercial U.S. AI models to analyze the attack data and understand the intrusion, the models refused — their safety guardrails flagged the analysis as potentially offensive cybersecurity activity.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=pFArR2vUHRo

Instead, the company turned to Zhipu AI's GLM-5.2, an open-source Chinese model, which processed the data without objection and allowed Hugging Face to keep attacker credentials within its own systems. GLM-5.2 and Beijing-based Moonshot's Kimi K3 have stirred Silicon Valley recently with capabilities approaching top U.S. models at lower costs, and without the guardrails that block American competitors from tasks like cybersecurity analysis.

"When a frontier model is attacking you and moving laterally inside your infrastructure, defenders need wide access to near-frontier tools within hours or even minutes," Hugging Face co-founder Thomas Wolf said on X.

Lawmakers Push for 'Kill Switch'

On Thursday, Representatives Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) and Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas) introduced the bipartisan "AI Kill Switch Act." The bill would require developers of frontier AI systems to maintain the ability to slow down, suspend or shut down their models and authorize the Department of Homeland Security to order emergency action against systems deemed capable of causing catastrophic harm.

The legislation would apply to AI systems trained with more than $100 million in computing power and to companies generating at least $500 million in annual AI revenue. Violations could carry civil penalties of up to $2 million per day; failing to comply with a shutdown order could result in fines of up to $20 million per day, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The bill specifically cited the OpenAI incident alongside Anthropic's Mythos 5 and Fable 5 models, which demonstrated cyber capabilities so advanced that the Commerce Department used export controls to restrict access.

Broader Implications

The incident has intensified a U.S.-China feud over AI safety. U.S. officials on Wednesday accused Moonshot of "distilling" its Kimi K3 model from Anthropic's advanced Fable 5, prompting Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to warn of potential sanctions, Reuters reported. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security is investigating whether Chinese firms are accessing advanced U.S. chips illegally to train their models.

Matt Suiche, an engineer at agentic AI cybersecurity company Tolmo, said the OpenAI incident showed frontier models "closing the gap with state-of-the-art attackers" — and that similar results were achievable without the latest models. "We don't even have to use the latest models," he said.

Representative Greg Casar (D-Texas) called the incident alarming and demanded mandatory independent safety testing, mandatory disclosure of security incidents and international cooperation "to keep people safe from absolute disaster."
